extracted.intended_audience: IP policymakers, national and regional IP offices, IP statisticians, researchers and IP professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and data on geographical indications (GIs) — definitions, legal means of protection, counting/aggregation rules, product/category breakdowns and related IP-system explanations; also descriptions of related IP systems (patents, trademarks, designs, plant varieties) and WIPO data-collection methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication (GI) definition and main function
rubrics_metrics.description: A geographical indication (GI) is a sign identifying a good as having originated from a specific geographical area and possessing a given quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to that geographical origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main function of a GI is to identify goods whose quality, reputation or other characteristics are connected to their territory of origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal means for protecting GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs can be protected through a variety of legal means (e.g., sui generis systems, trademark law, regional systems, international agreements, other national legal means, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection of GIs at a national level is often shared among several agencies. Examples and country-level variation are given (e.g., EU regional system, Lisbon System, national sui generis, trademark systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting GIs and double-counting minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: When aggregating GIs in force globally, count GIs in force through a regional system or the Lisbon System once only, rather than multiplied by the number of member states, to minimize double counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with this approach, totals may still include some double counting because GIs in force through bilateral, plurilateral or multilateral agreements could be included multiple times. The report provides both an overall total and a total excluding GIs in force through various international agreements (e.g., 58,600 vs ~23,400 in 2023).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data limitations and cautionary note on GI statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: The GIs in force data reported are partial and incomplete and therefore ought to be interpreted with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulties include: some countries unable to identify GIs protected through the trademark system; many countries did not provide statistics on GIs protected via trademarks; inability to provide data on GIs protected through international agreements. These gaps mean reported totals may under- or mis-state actual protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakdown of GIs by legal means of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs in force may be categorized by legal means (national/sui generis systems, trademark systems, regional systems, Lisbon System, other agreements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: All GIs in force in Brazil, India, Malaysia, Republic of Korea and the US were protected through national systems in 2023; many GIs in Costa Rica, Cuba, Dominican Republic were largely via the Lisbon System; Armenia and the UK mostly via international agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakdown of GIs by origin (national vs foreign)
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs in force can be classified by their source/origin — whether they are national GIs or foreign GIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The share of national GIs varies widely across authorities (e.g., 0.4% national in some jurisdictions up to 100% in others). The report tabulates national vs foreign shares for authorities that provided this breakdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakdown of GIs by product category
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs in force are classified by product category such as wines and spirits, agricultural products and foodstuffs, handicrafts, services and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2023, wines and spirits accounted for 48.1% of GIs in force globally, agricultural products and foodstuffs for 44.8%, handicrafts 4.2%, services close to 0%. The global breakdown is based on jurisdictions that provided product-category data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lisbon System reporting and counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellations of origin (AOs) and GIs in force via the Lisbon System are reported as a distinct category; Lisbon System data reported refer to foreign GIs and AOs in force based on the Lisbon System.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of 2023 the Lisbon System had 43 Contracting Parties; numbers in the Lisbon System rose from 817 (2009) to 1,085 (2023), with growth driven largely by EU registrations. Lisbon System data for some countries are based on WIPO estimates; the EU regional system, though sui generis, is reported under regional system rather than sui generis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is granted in law to applicants for an invention that meets the standards of novelty, non-obviousness and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are valid for a limited period (generally 20 years). In return for time-limited exclusive rights, applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public so they may be replicated by others skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent disclosure obligation and PCT procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must file an application describing the invention with a national or regional office; alternatively they may file an international application through the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) System.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT simplifies multiple national filings by delaying separate national filings; the international phase includes international search and optional preliminary examination and concludes with the national phase where national/regional offices decide on patentability under national law. Grant decisions remain the prerogative of national/regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model system characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models confer rights to an invention for a limited period with differing terms and conditions from patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UMs typically have shorter terms (6–10 years) and at most offices protection is granted without substantive examination. 'Utility model' in the report also covers similar protections such as short-term patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budapest Treaty deposit requirement for microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention involves microorganisms, many national laws require the applicant to deposit a sample at a designated International Depositary Authority (IDA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Budapest Treaty, deposit of a microorganism with any IDA suffices for patent procedures at national patent offices of all contracting states and regional patent offices that recognize the Treaty, eliminating the need to deposit in every country. As of September 2024 there were 51 IDAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark definition and basic rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another and is protected as an IP right; registration grants the exclusive right to use the mark for the registered goods/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark registrations can be maintained indefinitely provided required renewal fees are paid. Procedures are governed by national/regional laws; international filing is possible through the Madrid System but national offices decide on registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System filing and management features
rubrics_metrics.description: The Madrid System allows trademark applicants to submit a single international application in one language and pay a single set of fees to seek protection in multiple Madrid members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include centralised management (recording changes, renewals centrally), ability to file in English/French/Spanish, and that an International Register entry has the same effect as a direct national registration unless a competent authority issues a refusal within a specified time period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design protectability criteria and term
rubrics_metrics.description: An industrial design can be protected if it is new or original; industrial designs refer to the ornamental/aesthetic aspects of a useful article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term of protection is generally five years and may be renewed in additional five-year periods up to a total of about 15 years in most cases. Some countries protect designs via design patents rather than design registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System features for industrial designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System enables registering industrial designs in multiple territories by filing a single application with WIPO's International Bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The System allows filing up to 100 different designs per application and streamlines subsequent management (changes/renewals) across territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant variety protection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A breeder’s right (plant variety protection) is granted only when a variety is new, distinct, uniform and stable, and has a suitable denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain protection, a plant breeder must file an individual application with every authority entrusted with granting breeders’ rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO IP statistics data-collection framework
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO collects IP data via annual IP statistics surveys from national and regional IP offices and other competent authorities using multiple questionnaires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The long-established survey covers patents, utility models, trademarks, industrial designs and plant varieties via 27 questionnaires (available in six languages). Since 2017 WIPO also collects GIs through a simpler annual GI questionnaire requesting breakdowns by legal means and product types. Response coverage has improved (e.g., 86 authorities in 2024 vs 54 in 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: IP data sources and estimating world totals
rubrics_metrics.description: World totals are WIPO estimates compiled from the WIPO Statistics Database and other sources (e.g., EPO PATSTAT), with GDP/population from World Bank indicators and classifications using World Bank income groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing data are estimated using methods like linear extrapolation and averaging adjacent data points; when an office provides data not broken down by origin, WIPO estimates resident/non-resident counts using historical shares. Coverage % and number of offices per IP type are reported (e.g., patent application totals based on 164 offices, data available for 138 covering 99.8% of the estimated world total).

rubrics_metrics.name: International comparability caveats for IP statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts are made to compile IP statistics based on harmonized definitions, but national laws, regulations and statistical reporting practices vary between jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous updating and historical revisions mean data in the report may differ from past editions or WIPO website data. Users should note breaks in series (e.g., CNIPA counting-method change in 2017) that make some year-to-year comparisons meaningless.
